intent: Constrain a type graph with five linked rules — single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion — so that change stays local and every substitution point is a declared contract.
problem: A change to one requirement forces edits and retests across the whole program because a module has several unrelated reasons to change (SRP), subclasses weaken their base contract (LSP), clients are handed fat interfaces they mostly ignore (ISP), and high-level policy is compiled against concrete low-level detail (DIP).
context: Applies when a codebase's cost of change is dominated by ripple effects: touching one class rebuilds and re-verifies half the tree, mocking a concrete third-party type in a test requires reaching past the code under test, and extending behaviour means editing released classes instead of adding new ones. The principles are met as a family and used as refactoring pressure — SRP drives the extraction, DIP gives the extracted seam, LSP and ISP keep the seam substitutable.
benefits: Change impact stays bounded because each module has one reason to change, so recompilation, retest and redeploy blast radius shrinks.
New behaviour is added by introducing new types rather than editing released ones, which lowers regression risk in long-lived systems.
Subtypes can be swapped without breaking callers, so test doubles and alternate implementations are cheap and safe.
Clients depend on the narrowest interface they actually use, which shrinks the surface that must stay stable.
Policy is expressed against abstractions, so infrastructure can be replaced (in-memory for real, fake for test) without touching domain logic.
tradeoffs: Indirection tax: abstraction layers, injected interfaces and extra files make trace-from-entry-point to logic longer and stack traces deeper.
SRP is the hardest to get right — "responsibility" means reason to change, and naively one-class-one-job produces a swarm of anemic helpers.
DIP plus a DI container turns type-level errors into runtime wiring errors, losing the compiler check that plain direct construction gives.
ISP taken literally to one-method-per-interface produces marker-heavy hierarchies that are harder to navigate, not easier.
Applying all five up front on a small, stable problem is speculative overhead — the pay-off is deferred refactoring cost, not immediate speed.
Substitutability constrains what subclasses may do; LSP compliance can forbid optimizations (reordering, caching, relaxing preconditions) that would otherwise be safe for internal callers.
quality_attributes_note: simplicity 4 because the classic form adds layers; extensibility 9 because OCP+ISP+DPD are exactly extension points. coupling not scored. type_safety high only where interfaces are nominal (Java/C#); in structural languages DIP is unenforced at runtime.
performance_notes: Abstractions usually cost little directly, but virtual dispatch, interface-map lookups (Go) or boxing across a widened interface can dominate hot paths. Profile before replacing an interface with a concrete type; prefer generic/static dispatch (Rust, C++ templates, Scala) when the hot path is known.

participants.responsibility: The module, class or package whose dependency structure is being constrained.
participants.notes: The "unit" is whatever the language treats as one deployable/compilable unit — SRP is about reasons to change of that unit.

participants.responsibility: The consumer of the unit; ISP and DIP protect it.
participants.notes: ISP is measured from the client side, not from the implementer side.

participants.responsibility: The contract both sides depend on (interface, protocol, trait, type class).
participants.notes: Must be owned by the client side of the dependency, not by the implementation package.

participants.responsibility: The seam where new behaviour enters without editing released code.
participants.notes: Add a new implementation, never a switch statement inside the existing one.

use_cases: Splitting a god object that both computes a fee and renders a report into a domain calculator plus a presenter.
Replacing a hard-coded vendor SDK call behind an interface so tests can inject a stub.
Splitting a FatInterface with 40 methods that only two callers use into per-consumer interfaces.
Sealing a base class that was being subclassed for behaviour it never promised to support.
Building a pluggable storage port so the domain layer never imports an ORM.
avoid_when: The problem is stable, tiny and self-contained — five abstractions over a three-line function is pure overhead.
A compiler-enforced static-dispatch language (Rust, Haskell) already gives you substitutability without a hierarchy.
The dominant cost is latency inside a known hot loop, where virtual dispatch or an extra allocation per call is measurable.
Your language dispatches structurally (Python, JavaScript, Go) and you have no type discipline to violate in the first place.
pitfalls: Reading SRP as "one method per class" instead of "one reason to change per module" produces anemic helper classes with no cohesion.
Putting the abstraction in the concrete package so both sides depend on the same artifact — that is not inversion, it is just a rename.
DI containers hide missing registrations until the first call in production; prefer constructor defaults or explicit wiring.
Interface segregation applied to public API libraries of unknown clients leads to interface explosion.
Subclassing for reuse rather than for substitutability quietly breaks LSP; prefer composition (decorator, strategy) when behaviour is not a genuine is-a.

related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy is the OCP workhorse: variation goes into a swappable collaborator instead of a subclass.
related_patterns_notes.dependency-injection: DIP is the principle; dependency injection is the usual construction mechanism for it.
related_patterns_notes.layer-supertype: Layer Supertype defines the abstract contract that makes Liskov substitution meaningful for a whole layer at once.
related_patterns_notes.traits: Traits give the same SOLID benefits without a nominal hierarchy, which is why they are a natural fit in Rust and Scala.

anti_patterns: SOLID as a review checklist that produces one empty marker interface per class.
A "Manager" or "Handler" class that resolves every dependency from a global container, satisfying DIP in form while coupling to the container everywhere.
Deep interface chains created only to satisfy ISP, so callers depend on five collaborators instead of one.
Treating "closed for modification" as "never edit this file" instead of "change is not required here".
Breaking LSP with a subclass that tightens preconditions or adds observable side effects its base never had.
design_principles: Single reason to change per module (Martin, 1995/2014).
Open for extension, closed for modification (Bertrand Meyer, restated by Martin).
Subtypes must be substitutable for their bases without changing program correctness.
Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use.
Depend on abstractions; abstractions should not depend on details, details should depend on abstractions.
Policy separated from mechanism; composition preferred over inheritance.
best_practices: Treat SOLID as refactoring targets discovered by pain, not as up-front ceremony.
Name interfaces after the role the client needs, and keep them in the consuming package.
Add an automated test that proves substitutability before adding a second implementation.
When a language dispatches structurally, still declare the contract explicitly (Protocol, interface, JSDoc) so the intent survives.
Resist the zero-implementation-interface reflex; a marker interface encodes nothing.
Break inheritance chains with composition the moment LSP pressure appears.

Craig Larman, Protected Variation: The Importance of Being Closed, IEEE Software 18(2), 2001 — https://martinfowler.com/ieeeSoftware/protectedVariation.pdf
